subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection native foliage shrub

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring once the soil has warmed; this native bush honeysuckle selection tolerates most garden soils and needs little supplemental feeding once rooted in.

directions: Syrah GardenScape is a compact selection of the North American native shrub Diervilla, chosen for a tidy clumping habit and strong seasonal foliage color that shifts from bronze in spring to orange-red tones by autumn. Small summer flowers draw in pollinators, and the plant otherwise asks for little beyond occasional moisture during establishment. Grow it in sun to light shade in average, well-drained soil, and skip routine fertilizing since it performs best on a lean diet. Its deer resistance and heat tolerance make it a low-fuss filler for massed plantings or mixed borders.
sources: Sunset Western Garden Collection official site

subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection native foliage shrub

planting.note: Plant in spring in ordinary, well-drained soil; this compact Diervilla hybrid adapts to most native soils and rarely needs corrective pruning.

directions: Merlot GardenScape is a bred-for-color bush honeysuckle that opens the growing season with bronze new growth before cycling through orange, red, and finally deep burgundy shades as fall approaches. It stays compact and clumping at maturity, making it a manageable substitute for larger wild Diervilla species in foundation plantings or accent groupings. Average garden soil, sun to part shade, and minimal fertilizer are all it requires, and it tolerates heat and deer pressure well once established. Little to no pruning is needed to keep its natural form attractive.

common_name: Rose Gold Luxe Weigela (Golden-Foliage Pink-Flowered Weigela)
scientific_name: Weigela x hybrida PPAF (Rose Gold Luxe)

planting.note: Transplant in spring into well-drained garden soil; its naturally compact frame means it needs little to no shaping to stay dense and rounded.

directions: Rose Gold Luxe holds bright golden foliage through the heat of summer, a backdrop for pink spring flowers that return in smaller flushes later in the season. Its naturally dwarf, rounded habit fits small borders and container groupings without the hard pruning larger weigelas demand. Site it in full sun for the clearest gold color, since shade dulls the foliage toward green, and give it evenly moist but well-drained soil. It draws pollinators readily and shrugs off deer browsing better than many flowering shrubs.

common_name: Ebony Luxe Weigela (Glossy Dark-Foliage Pink Weigela)

planting.note: Set out in spring in average, well-drained soil; its glossy dark leaves and compact size suit it to small borders and mixed containers alike.

directions: Ebony Luxe carries unusually glossy, near-black foliage that holds its sheen through summer heat, contrasted against rosy-pink blooms that open heavily in spring and trickle back sporadically afterward. The compact, dense habit needs little pruning to stay tidy, making it useful for smaller gardens where older weigela cultivars would outgrow their space. Plant in full sun to light shade and keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged for best performance. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit the flowers readily, and the plant tolerates deer browsing well.

common_name: Bohemian Beauty Leucothoe (Tricolor Variegated Coastal Doghobble)
subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection evergreen shrub

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this coastal doghobble selection tolerates wet sites better than most shade shrubs.

directions: Bohemian Beauty is a tricolor leucothoe whose new growth emerges blushed in pink, green, and white before settling into a calmer variegated pattern, with small white bell flowers opening in spring. The arching evergreen habit works well in shaded foundation plantings, borders, or mass plantings where its color stands out against darker greens. It prefers humus-rich, acidic soil and tolerates occasional wet spots better than many broadleaf evergreens, though it still needs good drainage overall. Deer tend to leave it alone, and established plants need very little routine care beyond an occasional thinning cut.

common_name: Magic Mona Pink Plectranthus (Shade-Loving Pink-Flowered Spurflower)
subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection shade perennial

planting.note: Set out after the last frost in a shaded bed, basket, or container with rich, well-drained soil; indoors it can be grown as a houseplant year-round.

directions: Magic Mona Pink is a shade-tolerant plectranthus bred for bright color in low-light spots where most flowering plants struggle, blooming from fall into winter in mild climates. Its compact, clumping habit suits hanging baskets, shaded borders, and mass plantings, and it adapts readily to life as an indoor houseplant where winters turn frosty. Keep it in evenly moist, well-drained soil and feed from spring through fall to sustain steady growth. Trim spent flower stems back after bloom to encourage another round of color.

common_name: Magic Mona Purple Plectranthus (Shade-Loving Purple-Flowered Spurflower)
scientific_name: Plectranthus Hybrid 'De Wet F' PP31501 (Magic Mona Purple)
subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection shade perennial

planting.note: Set out after the last frost in a shaded spot with rich, well-drained soil; further north it performs well as a potted houseplant brought indoors for winter.

directions: Magic Mona Purple pairs glossy dark-green leaves with purple undersides against spikes of lavender-purple flowers, giving it two-toned appeal even before it blooms. It handles heat well for a shade plant and keeps a neat, clumping form that fits baskets, borders, and mixed containers without sprawling. Grow it in evenly moist, fertile, well-drained soil out of direct sun, and feed lightly through the growing season to keep flowering steady. North of its hardiness range it overwinters easily indoors as a houseplant.
sources: Sunset Western Garden Collection official site

subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection water-wise perennial

planting.note: Divide and plant clumps in spring in well-drained, average soil; established plantings need little supplemental water beyond occasional deep soaks.

directions: Purpleicious is a society garlic selection grown as much for its year-round purple-striped foliage as for its clusters of lilac-pink, garlic-scented flowers. Both the leaves and blooms are edible with a mild garlic-onion flavor, letting it double as an ornamental edging plant and a casual kitchen herb. It thrives in lean, sharply drained soil and needs very little water once its clumping roots establish, making it a reliable choice for water-wise borders and coastal gardens. Deer generally avoid it, and division every few years keeps clumps vigorous.

common_name: Tinto Sangria Mandevilla (Deep Red Trellis Mandevilla)
subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection flowering vine

planting.note: Plant after the last frost near a trellis, pergola, or large container with rich, well-drained soil; it can also be grown as an annual or overwintered houseplant outside its hardiness range.

directions: Tinto Sangria was bred specifically for California growing conditions, producing deep red trumpet flowers against glossy dark foliage from spring through fall. Its naturally branching habit covers a trellis or arbor with minimal pinching compared to older mandevilla cultivars, making vertical training easier for home gardeners. Give it full sun to light shade, well-drained soil, and regular feeding during the growing season for continuous bloom. In climates with hard winters, grow it in a container and bring it indoors or treat it as a summer annual.
sources: Sunset Western Garden Collection official site

subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection flowering vine

planting.note: Plant after the last frost at the base of a trellis or in a large pot with rich, well-drained soil; it also performs well as a potted houseplant overwintered indoors.

directions: Rosé Sangria is a California-bred mandevilla that smothers itself in clear pink flowers against deep green, glossy leaves from spring through fall. Like other naturally branching mandevilla selections, it fills out a trellis or arbor with little pinching needed to encourage coverage. It performs best in full sun to part shade with well-drained soil and benefits from regular feeding through the warm months. Where winters bring hard frost, keep it in a container so it can be moved indoors or grown as a seasonal annual.

common_name: Misty River Osmanthus (Pink-and-White Variegated Fragrant Tea Olive)
subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection evergreen shrub

planting.note: Plant in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to shade; it can be grown as a large shrub or limbed up into a small multi-stemmed tree.

directions: Misty River stands out among fragrant tea olives for its new foliage splashed in pink, white, and green rather than the plain dark green of the species, paired with the same sweetly scented small flowers that open from fall through early spring. It flowers notably well even as a young plant, which is unusual for osmanthus and rewards gardeners with fragrance sooner than most cultivars. Grow it in organically rich, well-drained soil in filtered light, where it has shown better cold tolerance than many variegated tea olive selections. Train it as a dense screening shrub or prune up the lower growth for a small accent tree.

common_name: Green Breeze Garden Clouds Lonicera (Boxwood-Alternative Box Honeysuckle)
scientific_name: Lonicera nitida 'GRLN01' PP33591 (Green Breeze Garden Clouds)
subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection evergreen shrub

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in sun to light shade; feed with a balanced slow-release fertilizer each spring to keep the dense, shearable form filling in.

directions: Green Breeze is a disease-resistant box honeysuckle bred as a stand-in for traditional boxwood, carrying the same small, glossy, bright green leaves on a naturally rounded frame. It shears easily into tight hedges, balls, or edging shapes without the blight and leafminer problems that plague many boxwoods today. The plant grows quickly compared to true boxwood, filling in borders, foundation plantings, and mass plantings in less time. Average well-drained soil and a yearly spring feeding are all it needs to stay dense and healthy.
sources: Sunset Western Garden Collection official site

common_name: Purple Storm Garden Clouds Lonicera (Purple-New-Growth Box Honeysuckle)
scientific_name: Lonicera nitida 'GRLN02' PP33761 (Purple Storm Garden Clouds)
subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection evergreen shrub

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil anywhere from full sun to shade; feed yearly in spring with a balanced slow-release fertilizer.

directions: Purple Storm adds dark purple flushes on its new shoots to the same small, glossy green leaves that make box honeysuckle a popular boxwood substitute. It keeps a naturally rounded, dense form that takes well to shearing for hedges, edging, or formal accents, and it tolerates both full sun and considerable shade better than true boxwood. Plant it in ordinary well-drained soil and expect fast establishment compared to slower broadleaf evergreens. A single spring feeding with a balanced fertilizer is generally all the extra care it needs.
sources: Sunset Western Garden Collection official site

common_name: Copper Glow Garden Clouds Lonicera (Copper-New-Growth Box Honeysuckle)
scientific_name: Lonicera nitida 'GRLN03' PP33592 (Copper Glow Garden Clouds)
subcategory: Sunset Western Garden Collection evergreen shrub

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in sun to part shade; shear as needed to keep its naturally rounded boxwood-alternative form tidy.

directions: Copper Glow shows off bright copper-toned new growth against its otherwise glossy green foliage, adding seasonal color interest to a box honeysuckle that is already prized as a tougher boxwood alternative. Its fast, dense growth fills in borders, low hedges, and rock garden plantings quickly while resisting the diseases that have made true boxwood harder to grow reliably. Plant in well-drained garden soil with a yearly spring feeding, and shear or shape as desired since it does not flower and has no bloom season to protect. It adapts to a wide range of light conditions, from full sun to considerable shade.

common_name: Dark Side of the Moon Lunar Lights Begonia (Dark-Foliage Red-Flowered Begonia)
scientific_name: Begonia Hybrid 'Dark Side of the Moon' PP34859

planting.note: Plant after the last frost in a partly shaded bed or container with moist, well-drained soil; it dies back in winter at the cold end of its range and regrows from the roots in spring.

directions: Dark Side of the Moon is a Lunar Lights begonia grown for its dark, glossy foliage that cascades outward into generous mounded clumps, topped from late spring until frost by bright red flowers. The strong color contrast between the foliage and blooms makes it a standout in shaded borders, containers, and mass plantings where subtler begonias can get lost. Grow it in moist, well-drained soil out of direct sun, and give it a balanced slow-release feeding in spring to support its fast-growing, bushy habit. No pruning is required beyond occasional tidying, and it returns reliably from its roots each spring within its hardiness range.
